title: Patacara
hook: she loses husband, children and parents in one day and runs wild; the Buddha says, sister, recover your mind

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kisa Gotami: every house had one, and every house had known death. Your line was no house is untouched. Day seventy-six.

This week is hard stories, and today's is the hardest to hear, so breathe as you listen. There's a kind of overwhelm that isn't one blow but many, landing before you've gotten up from the last. People who've lived through a disaster, or a terrible year, know it. The mind just can't hold any more. Patacara was the daughter of a wealthy family in Savatthi. She fell in love with a servant in her parents' house and ran away with him, and they lived poor, far from her family. When she was expecting their second child, she set out with her husband and little son to walk home to her parents. And a storm came.
screen: `BREATHE AS YOU LISTEN.` → `NOT ONE BLOW, BUT MANY.` → `A WALK HOME, AND A STORM.`

segments.voice: The story, told in the commentaries, is very hard, so we'll tell it plainly and briefly. In the storm, she gives birth by the road. Her husband goes to find branches for shelter, and a snake bites him, and he dies. In the morning, with a newborn and a toddler, she reaches a river swollen with rain. She carries the baby across first, lays him on the far bank, and turns back for her older son. A hawk swoops toward the baby. She waves and shouts to scare it off. And her little boy, on the other bank, thinks she's calling him, steps into the river, and is swept away. The hawk takes the baby. She walks on to Savatthi, and at the city a traveler tells her that in the night's storm her parents' house fell, and her mother, father and brother were killed. She can see the smoke of their cremation. Her mind breaks. She runs through the streets, her clothes falling away, and people throw dirt at her and chase her off. She runs into the grove where the Buddha is teaching. People try to stop her. He says, let her come. And when she's near, he says to her: sister, recover your mind. That's all. Sister. Not madwoman. Not sinner. Sister. And something in her comes back. She sees herself. Someone throws her a cloak. She sits at his feet and tells him everything. He listens. He doesn't tell her it didn't happen. He tells her that across the long round of lives, the tears shed for loved ones are more than the water in the oceans. She isn't alone in it. Patacara became a nun, and in time a teacher of other women. Her own verses survive in the Therigatha, the verses of the early nuns, and beside them are verses from women who came to her grieving.
screen: `A STORM, A SNAKE, A RIVER.` · `SHE RUNS WILD THROUGH THE CITY.` · `SISTER, RECOVER YOUR MIND.` · `A TEACHER OF WOMEN WHO LOST.` · then, large: `RECOVER YOUR MIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: steady your breath when overwhelmed, and practice it now, while it's calm. Settle. Put one hand on your chest. Breathe in for four, slowly. Hold for a moment. Breathe out for six. Again. Let the out-breath be longer than the in-breath, every time. If you like, let a word ride on it, the way Patacara heard one word: sister. You're learning the way back, so it's there when you need it. The bell holds the time.
Patacara. The woman who lost everyone in a day, ran wild with grief, heard the words, sister, recover your mind, and became a teacher of women.
Your line: recover your mind. Today, when things pile up, put a hand on your chest and take one long out-breath before the next thing. Day seventy-six.

howItsDone: Buddhists remember Patacara as a great nun and teacher of women, honored for her mastery of the monastic discipline, and her verses and those of her students are preserved in the Therigatha.

fork.setup: a woman runs into the grove, wild with grief, clothes falling away. people try to drive her off. you're the teacher. what do you do?

fork.reveal: he says let her come, and says: sister, recover your mind. she comes back to herself, and someone gives her a cloak.

original.note: Pali: sister. What the Buddha called Patacara as she came toward him.

trapdoor: what you thought: a tragedy with a happy ending tacked on.
what it means: a woman whose mind broke under grief, met with one kind word, who became a teacher of other grieving women.
what a scholar hears: Dhammapada commentary on verse 113 and the Therigatha commentary; her verses are Therigatha 112–116; 'recover your mind' renders satim patilabha: get back your presence of mind.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 15.3 (tears more than the four oceans)

notes: Sensitive: deaths of a husband, two children and parents. Told plainly and briefly; Keeper to confirm tone and whether any detail (people throwing dirt) should be cut.
The story is commentarial; details (snake bite, the Aciravati river, the hawk, the collapsed house) follow the Dhammapada commentary. Confirm.
The tears-and-oceans teaching attributed to the Buddha's words to her follows the commentary, which draws on the Assu Sutta (SN 15.3). Confirm.
'Recover your mind' = satim patilabha, bhagini (commentary). Confirm Pali.
Patacara as expert in Vinaya and teacher of many women (Thig 117–121 are her students' verses; later tradition mentions 500). Confirm.
